The Real Risk Isn't Being Wrong. It's Assuming the Game Stops Moving

Walking into rooms at UCLA where I wasn't the expert taught me more than any framework did.

EssayJanuary 26, 20262 min read
#Learning#UCLAAnderson

Here's a fascinating truth in sports: the moment you think you've mastered the game is often the moment you start falling behind. Not because your performance drops, but because the baseline of excellence keeps moving forward.

That idea has stayed with me. After many years in industry, I came to UCLA Anderson expecting most of my learning to come from new frameworks and tools. Instead, some of the most meaningful growth has come from deliberately walking into rooms where I wasn't the most familiar with the subject.

Over the past two years, I've worked alongside medical, law, and public policy students across sustainability initiatives, non-profit consulting projects and much more. What stood out wasn't just the difference in how people think, but how openly they shared what they knew, while remaining equally curious about perspectives outside their own field. That combination is rare, and powerful.

John Wooden said success is the peace of mind that comes from knowing you gave your absolute best. That idea is liberating. It removes the pressure of always needing to have all the answers, and replaces it with something more valuable: curiosity.

In the long run, the real risk isn't being wrong. It's assuming the game stops moving.
